title: Founder dilution math: why ~5% is the typical final stake in VC-backed startups
summary: Levels uses Carta median data to show how each funding round and each co-founder shrinks a founder's stake, then converts that into expected payouts at a $1B exit, a median $71M exit, and probability-weighted outcomes. His point: VC is a moonshot game, and the typical founder ends with a small slice of a small exit.

principles.text: Funding is never free: every round sells a slice of the company, and you only win if the remaining part is worth more.
principles.quote: Raising money is not free, people don't give you money out of charity, they buy a little slice of your company every time they invest

principles.text: Dilution plus co-founders pushes the typical VC-backed founder's final stake down to around 5%.
principles.quote: ~5% ownership probably the most common final % most VC funded startups will have when they work out, especially when you have a co-founder

principles.text: Judge outcomes realistically: median exit values are far below the billion-dollar headline numbers.
principles.quote: the median acquisition value for a VC-backed startup sits at approximately $71 million

principles.text: Most startups never get acquired, so probability-weighted expected payouts are much smaller than the exit figures suggest.
principles.quote: most startups are by definition doomed to fail, only ~15% of startups ever get acquired

principles.text: VC is a high-variance path chosen for the rare huge payout, not a bad deal; know the math before taking it.
principles.quote: VC-backed startups shoot for the moon, it's one of the few ways you can have a crazy big payout and become an actual billionaire

principles.text: Bootstrapping with your own money makes billionaire-scale outcomes rare, but you keep ownership.
principles.quote: which is very rare as a bootstrapped founder with your own money!
